## Question 135: A Lower Endpoint for Recording Delays

::: {.exam-prompt}

A recorder has an unknown minimum startup delay $\theta\geq 0$ seconds. Independent
startup times $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ have density
$$
f(x\mid\theta)=
\begin{cases}
2e^{-2(x-\theta)}, & x\geq\theta,\\
0, & x<\theta.
\end{cases}
$$
Use the stated value of the density at $x=\theta$.

(a) Write down the likelihood for a sample $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ and give the
    range of $\theta$ on which it is positive.

(b) Derive the maximum likelihood estimator of $\theta$. Explain how the
    likelihood behaves on its positive range.

(c) Find the estimate for the observed times $2.4$, $2.1$, $3.8$, and $2.9$
    seconds. An analyst proposes using the sample mean instead. Explain what
    likelihood that proposal gives for these observations.

:::

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Every observation must satisfy $x_i\geq\theta$. For a sample from
this model, write $x_{(1)}=\min_i x_i\geq 0$. Independence gives
$$
L(\theta)=
\begin{cases}
2^n\exp\!\left(-2\sum_{i=1}^n x_i+2n\theta\right), & 0\leq\theta\leq x_{(1)},\\
0, & \theta>x_{(1)}.
\end{cases}
$$

**(b)** On $[0,x_{(1)}]$, the factor $\exp(2n\theta)$ is strictly increasing
in $\theta$. The stipulated density includes the endpoint, so the likelihood
attains its maximum at $\hat\theta=\min_i X_i$.

**(c)** The maximum likelihood estimate is $2.1$ seconds. The sample mean is
$2.8$ seconds. Using $\theta=2.8$ would assign density zero to the observed
times $2.1$ and $2.4$, so the joint likelihood at the sample mean is zero.

</details>

## Question 136: Credible Regions for Two Calibration Ranges

::: {.exam-prompt}

A calibration parameter $\theta$ has posterior density $0.4$ on each of the
intervals $[0,1]$ and $[3,4]$, and density $0.1$ on $(1,3)$. The density is
zero elsewhere. The following sets each contain $80\%$ posterior probability:
$$
C_1=[0.25,3.75],
\qquad
C_2=[0,1]\cup[3,4].
$$

(a) Explain what the quoted $80\%$ probability means and which of $C_1$ and
    $C_2$ can be called a credible interval.

(b) Use the definition of a highest-density region to determine which of these
    two sets is an $80\%$ highest-density region. Give a density comparison that
    rules out the other set.

(c) A technician reads $C_1$ as saying that the central range $(1,3)$ is where
    most of the posterior probability lies. Find the posterior probability of
    that range and explain how the two candidate sets can have the same
    probability despite covering different values.

:::

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Conditional on the prior, model and data used to obtain the posterior,
$\Pr(\theta\in C_j\mid\underline{x})=0.8$ for either set. Both sets are
credible regions. $C_1$ is an interval because it is connected, while $C_2$
consists of two disjoint intervals.

**(b)** A highest-density region contains the points with the greatest
posterior density up to the requested probability. For example, the density
threshold $0.2$ gives exactly $C_2$, which has probability $0.8$. By contrast,
$C_1$ includes $\theta=2$, where the density is $0.1$, while excluding
$\theta=0.1$, where it is $0.4$. No density threshold can include the former
without also including the latter.

**(c)** The central range has posterior probability $(3-1)(0.1)=0.2$. Relative
to $C_2$, $C_1$ includes this central range and omits two outer pieces of
length $0.25$ with density $0.4$. The pieces omitted have combined probability
$2(0.25)(0.4)=0.2$. The exchanged probability is the same.

</details>

## Question 137: A One-Sided Test for Mean Processing Time

::: {.exam-prompt}

A workshop wants to know whether a machine's mean processing time $\mu$ has
increased from $20$ minutes. Independent processing times $X_i$ have a Gamma
distribution with shape $4$ and rate $4/\mu$, so
$\mathrm{E}[X_i]=\mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=\mu^2/4$. The mean of $n=64$
observations is $22.5$ minutes. Use a $5\%$ level and take the standard Normal
CDF value $\Phi(2)\approx 0.97725$.

(a) State the hypotheses and use the Central Limit Theorem to give the
    approximate null distribution of the sample mean.

(b) Construct a standardised test statistic, compute the observed value and
    $p$-value, and state the decision in context.

(c) Explain what a Type I error would mean for the workshop and why the
    calculation in (b) uses the upper tail.

:::

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The hypotheses are $H_0:\mu=20$ and $H_1:\mu>20$. The observations
are i.i.d. with finite variance. Under $H_0$, the Central Limit Theorem
therefore gives
$$
\bar X\ \overset{\mathrm{approx.}}{\sim}\
\mathcal N\!\left(20,\frac{20^2}{4\cdot 64}\right).
$$
The null standard error is $20/\sqrt{4\cdot 64}=1.25$ minutes.

**(b)** The statistic $Z=(\bar X-20)/1.25$ is approximately standard Normal
under $H_0$. Its observed value is $(22.5-20)/1.25=2$. The upper-tail
$p$-value is about $1-0.97725=0.02275$. Since $0.02275<0.05$, reject
$H_0$. The data provide evidence that the mean processing time has increased.

**(c)** A Type I error is concluding that the processing time has increased
when the true mean is $20$ minutes. The alternative concerns an increase, so
large positive values of $Z$ provide evidence in that direction.

</details>

## Question 138: Exact Size and Power for a Germination Test

::: {.exam-prompt}

A small greenhouse experiment uses five seeds. Each seed germinates
independently with probability $p$, so the count $X$ that germinates has a
$\mathrm{Binomial}(5,p)$ distribution. Test $H_0:p=0.4$ against $H_1:p>0.4$.
The proposed tests reject when $X\geq c$ for an integer cutoff $c$.

(a) Find the smallest cutoff giving a test of level $5\%$. Calculate the
    achieved size of this test.

(b) Four of the five seeds germinate. Find the exact one-sided $p$-value and
    state what the study can conclude about $p$ at the $5\%$ level.

(c) Find the power and the Type II error probability when $p=0.8$.

:::

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The null upper-tail probabilities at the two largest attainable
counts are
$$
\Pr_{0.4}(X\geq 4)=5(0.4)^4(0.6)+(0.4)^5=0.08704,
\qquad
\Pr_{0.4}(X\geq 5)=(0.4)^5=0.01024.
$$
Smaller cutoffs only increase the tail probability. Hence $c=5$ is the
smallest cutoff with size no more than $0.05$. Its achieved size is
$0.01024$ because $H_0$ specifies a single value of $p$.

**(b)** The $p$-value is $\Pr_{0.4}(X\geq4)=0.08704$. Fail to reject
$H_0$ at the $5\%$ level. The five observations give insufficient evidence
to conclude that the germination probability exceeds $0.4$.

**(c)** At $p=0.8$, power is the probability of reaching the same rejection
region, $\Pr_{0.8}(X=5)=(0.8)^5=0.32768$. The Type II error probability
at this alternative is $1-0.32768=0.67232$.

</details>

## Question 139: Updating the Rate at Which a Queue Clears

::: {.exam-prompt}

Four independent clearance times $X_i$, measured in minutes, have an
Exponential distribution with rate $\lambda>0$. Their observed total is
$12$ minutes. The prior for $\lambda$ is $\mathrm{Gamma}(3,2)$ in
shape–rate form. A $\mathrm{Gamma}(a,b)$ density is proportional to
$\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}$ and has mean $a/b$.

(a) Derive the posterior distribution of $\lambda$.

(b) Calculate the MAP estimate by maximising the log posterior.

(c) Calculate the posterior mean and express it as a weighted average of the
    prior mean and the maximum likelihood estimate from the clearance times.
    State what the weights are proportional to.

:::

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The likelihood is proportional to $\lambda^4e^{-12\lambda}$.
Multiplying by the prior kernel $\lambda^2e^{-2\lambda}$ gives
$\lambda^6e^{-14\lambda}$. Thus
$$
\lambda\mid\underline{x}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(7,14).
$$

**(b)** Up to a constant the log posterior is $6\log\lambda-14\lambda$.
Its derivative is $6/\lambda-14$, which vanishes at
$\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{MAP}}=6/14=3/7$ per minute. The second derivative
$-6/\lambda^2$ is negative on the positive half-line, so this is the maximum.

**(c)** The log-likelihood has derivative $4/\lambda-12$, so the MLE is
$4/12=1/3$ per minute. The prior mean is $3/2$ per minute and the posterior
mean is
$$
\mathrm{E}[\lambda\mid\underline{x}]
=\frac{7}{14}
=\frac{2}{14}\frac{3}{2}+\frac{12}{14}\frac{4}{12}
=0.5
$$
per minute. The weights are proportional to the prior rate hyperparameter $2$
and the total observed clearance time $12$.

</details>

## Question 140: A Posterior with a Bounded Prior

::: {.exam-prompt}

A sorting station diverts each inspected item to a manual check independently
with probability $p$. A mechanical limit ensures $0\leq p\leq 1/2$. The
prior density is $\pi(p)=8p$ on this closed interval and zero elsewhere.
In a short trial, both of two inspected items are diverted. Use the stated
closed support for the posterior density when evaluating its mode.

(a) Derive the normalised posterior density of $p$.

(b) Find the posterior mean and the MAP estimate.

(c) Find the prior and posterior probabilities of $p>1/4$. Interpret how
    observing the two diversions changes the probability of this event.

:::

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The observed data have likelihood $p^2$. Multiplying by the prior
gives $8p^3$ on $[0,1/2]$. This kernel integrates to
$8(1/2)^4/4=1/8$, so the posterior density is $64p^3$ on $[0,1/2]$ and
zero elsewhere.

**(b)** The posterior mean is
$$
\int_0^{1/2}p(64p^3)\,\mathrm{d}p
=\frac{64}{5}(1/2)^5=\frac25.
$$
The posterior density increases up to the included upper endpoint. The MAP
estimate is therefore $1/2$.

**(c)** Before the trial the probability is
$$
\Pr(p>1/4)=\int_{1/4}^{1/2}8p\,\mathrm{d}p
=4\bigl((1/2)^2-(1/4)^2\bigr)=\frac34.
$$
After the trial it is
$$
\Pr(p>1/4\mid\underline{x})=\int_{1/4}^{1/2}64p^3\,\mathrm{d}p
=16\bigl((1/2)^4-(1/4)^4\bigr)=\frac{15}{16}.
$$
Larger values of $p$ make two diversions more likely. The observations raise
the probability that the station diverts more than a quarter of the items,
from $0.75$ to $0.9375$.

</details>

## Question 141: Likelihood Ratio Evidence from Connection Attempts

::: {.exam-prompt}

A monitoring device records the number of attempts needed to connect after
each restart. Independently for each restart, this count $X_i$ has
probability mass function
$$
f(x\mid p)=p(1-p)^{x-1},\qquad x=1,2,\ldots,\quad 0<p<1.
$$
The technical specification assumes a success probability of $1/2$ on each
attempt. Test $H_0:p=1/2$ against $H_1:p\ne 1/2$. Write $S=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$,
and assume $S>n$ for the samples considered.

(a) Obtain the log-likelihood for $p$ and derive its maximum likelihood
    estimator.

(b) Express the likelihood ratio test statistic in terms of $n$, $S$ and the
    observed MLE. State its approximate null distribution for large $n$
    and the rejection rule at significance level $\alpha$.

(c) The device records a total of $S=150$ attempts across $n=60$ restarts.
    Compute the observed likelihood ratio statistic. Use the supplied
    quantiles to decide whether to reject at $5\%$ and at $1\%$. Give
    bounds on the approximate $p$-value and interpret the result at $5\%$.

(d) An independent run with $n=30$ and $S=75$ gives the same sample mean.
    Explain why the two runs have the same MLE but different test statistics.
    State whether the second run rejects at $5\%$ using the same approximation.

You may use $\log(0.8)\approx -0.22314$ and $\log(1.2)\approx 0.18232$.
The $0.95$ and $0.99$ quantiles of $\chi^2_1$ are $3.841$ and $6.635$,
respectively.

:::

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Independence gives $L(p)=p^n(1-p)^{S-n}$. The log-likelihood and
its first derivative are
$$
\ell(p)=n\log p +(S-n)\log(1-p),\qquad
\ell'(p)=\frac{n}{p}-\frac{S-n}{1-p}.
$$
Setting the derivative to zero gives $n(1-p)=(S-n)p$, or
$\hat p=n/S=1/\bar X$. This is an interior maximum since $S>n$ and $\ell$
is strictly concave.

**(b)** The likelihood ratio statistic is
$$
D=2\{\ell(\hat p)-\ell(1/2)\}
=2\left[n\log(2\hat p)+(S-n)\log\{2(1-\hat p)\}\right].
$$
Under the null, $D$ is approximately $\chi^2_1$ for large $n$. Reject
when $D$ exceeds the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $\chi^2_1$.

**(c)** Here $\hat p=60/150=0.4$ and
$$
D=2[60\log(0.8)+90\log(1.2)]\approx 6.04.
$$
Since $3.841<6.04<6.635$, reject at $5\%$ and fail to reject at $1\%$.
The approximate $p$-value lies between $0.01$ and $0.05$. At the $5\%$
level there is evidence that the success probability differs from the
specification of $1/2$. The fitted value is lower than the specification.

**(d)** Both runs give $\bar x=2.5$ and $\hat p=0.4$. The formula in (b)
has the same log terms for each run, but the coefficients $n$ and $S-n$ in
the second run are half as large. This gives $D\approx 3.02$, below $3.841$,
so the second run fails to reject at $5\%$. The likelihood accumulates
evidence from each restart, so the same estimate gives stronger evidence
in the larger sample.

</details>
